lessons.title: Conditioning flowers and foliage
lessons.html:
Conditioning flowers and foliage

When flowers arrive from the grower or market, they are often thirsty after travelling in boxes. Conditioning (also called hardening or processing) is the treatment that helps them drink water again, so they open well and last long. Every stem must be conditioned before it is sold or used in an arrangement.

Prepare

  • Wash buckets with detergent and the sanitiser your shop uses, and rinse.
  • Fill with clean, fresh water and the right amount of flower food, as the packet says.
  • Sharpen your florist knife or secateurs. Blunt tools crush stems so they cannot drink.

Basic conditioning steps

  1. Unpack carefully as soon as the flowers arrive. Remove rubber bands and wrapping that bruise stems.
  2. Remove lower leaves: any leaf that will be under water. Leaves in water rot and feed bacteria.
  3. Recut the stems by a few centimetres at a slant (angle). A slant cut gives more surface to drink and the stem does not sit flat on the bucket floor. Cut under water or put the stem in water straight away so air does not block it.
  4. Place in water at once, in the clean bucket.
  5. Rest: leave flowers in a cool place or cool room for a few hours before using them, so they drink fully.

Remove damage

  • Take off bruised or brown outer petals (guard petals on roses) only if damaged; they protect the bloom.
  • Remove thorns from the lower stem if your shop does it, without scraping the bark too deeply.
  • Throw away stems that are broken, slimy or diseased.

Record the date flowers came in, so older stock is used first.

lessons.title: Special treatments for different stems
lessons.html:
Special treatments

Different plant material needs different treatment. Your supervisor will show you the methods your shop uses. Common ones are:

TypeExamplesTreatment
Soft stemsGerberas, tulips, arumsSlant cut, shallow water. Gerberas can be supported in a grid so stems stay straight.
Woody stemsProteas, leucospermums (pincushions), shrubsCut at a slant with secateurs. Some florists also split the stem end. Remove lower leaves. Proteas are South African fynbos flowers; keep their leaves out of water and away from heat to slow leaf blackening.
Sappy or milky stemsEuphorbias, poppiesSap can block the stem. Sear the cut end in hot water or briefly with a flame, as your shop does, to seal it.
Bulb flowers that leak sapDaffodils, narcissusKeep them in their own bucket for some hours before mixing. Their sap harms other flowers.
Hollow stemsDelphiniums, amaryllisSome florists fill the stem with water and plug it.
Wilted flowersRoses that droopRecut and stand in deep water, sometimes wrapped in paper to keep stems straight while they drink.

Foliage

  • Remove lower leaves, recut stems and place in water.
  • Many foliages can be fully dipped in cool water to refresh, but not furry or grey leaves.

Safety

  • Cut away from your body and keep fingers behind the blade.
  • Some sap irritates skin and eyes, such as euphorbia sap. Wear gloves and do not rub your eyes. Wash hands after handling.
  • Be careful with hot water and flames when searing.
  • Use cleaning chemicals as the label says, with gloves.

Key points

  • Condition every stem before use: unpack, remove lower leaves, recut at a slant and place in clean water with flower food.
  • Use sharp tools so stems are not crushed.
  • Sear sappy stems, and keep daffodils apart before mixing.
  • Rest flowers in a cool place so they drink fully.
  • Wear gloves for irritating sap and wash your hands.
